questions.explanation: The definition in general use is a morphological one: an urban place is a continuously built-up area, and what makes it urban is that buildings are close enough together to form a single settlement rather than scattered holdings. The threshold is arbitrary but it has to be arbitrary, and what matters is that one number is fixed and applied to every place on the map. The other options each substitute a comparison for a threshold. Comparing inhabitants with a rural average moves the boundary every time a region's agriculture changes, so a settlement can enter or leave the urban category without a single new building. Listing amenities measures how well a place is served, which is a policy question, and many perfectly dense nineteenth-century settlements had no school at all. questions.explanation: The rank-size rule is a conditional claim. It says that if cities are laid out as a system in which each centre serves a hinterland requiring it, then each rank's size follows from its position in the ordering, and under the simplest version each city holds the largest city's population divided by its rank. Every part of that is an assumption, and a departure is information about which assumption fails in a particular place. A shortfall at rank three can arise because the country's transport network is oriented so that the third centre is bypassed, or because its hinterland is too small to support a city of the predicted size, or because a different centre has absorbed the trade that would sustain it. What the shortfall does not do is refute the rule everywhere, which is the first option's error, nor imply the observation is wrong, which is the third. A useful habit is to treat a departure as a prompt: it identifies a specific place and asks what is different there.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be true for the prediction to hold, then ask which of those things is not true here.

questions.explanation: Density in a city falls with distance from the centre in almost every large urban region, and the steepness of that fall is the gradient. Sprawl changes the gradient by extending the zone of low density outward: the same density that used to end the built-up area now sits twenty kilometres from the centre, so the distance over which density declines grows and the curve flattens. That flattening is the quantitative signature of sprawl, which is why it is measured rather than merely described. The second option has the direction backwards, because sprawl works by dispersing the population rather than concentrating it, and the third confuses a single regional average with a pattern across space: two regions can share an average density and have completely different gradients, one compact and one dispersed. The fourth is the extreme and unrealistic case. The gradient never inverts, because the centre retains the land uses that need proximity and access, so even a heavily sprawled region keeps its core above its own periphery.

questions.explanation: Compact growth is a bargain, and its whole point is that both sides of it are real. Concentrating population in the built-up area shortens the distance between homes, workplaces and services, so a resident covers fewer kilometres a day and the fixed cost of a road or a water main is spread across more people who use it. What the concentration consumes is per-capita space and the ability of the housing market to offer cheap land, because the supply of buildable land inside the boundary is finite and the demand for it is not. The second option describes the reverse policy exactly, which is why it is the most common error: low-density expansion does deliver garden space and cheaper land, and it does so by paying for it in kilometres and in infrastructure per resident. The third option is the belief that density is only a cartographic fact, and the fourth confuses compactness with a housing benefit it does not deliver. A council that adopts this policy has usually decided that transport and infrastructure savings are worth more to residents than extra private space.

questions.explanation: The decisive feature is the empty band. No housing at all was built between 15 and 25 kilometres, while 57 per cent went beyond 35 kilometres, so development was not spread outward continuously but jumped over an intermediate zone. That is the leapfrog pattern, and it appears wherever the intervening belt has something that blocks construction: a flood plain, a nature reserve, a former airfield, a pipeline easement, or a road that has become a barrier between two sides of the same belt. questions.explanation: A polycentric metropolitan region is one in which employment and activity have organised themselves around several centres rather than one, and the reason is agglomeration operating at more than one point. Firms gain from being near other firms, near skilled labour, and near transport, and once a cluster has formed somewhere else in the region, a firm choosing between two locations may prefer the second cluster even though the first is larger, because the marginal advantage of joining an established cluster can outweigh the advantage of joining the largest one. A new interchange, a university hospital, or an airport changes the accessibility of a place that was previously ordinary, and that is enough to start a second centre. The second option invents a cause that the pattern itself argues against, since nothing about a polycentric region requires anything to have been destroyed. The fourth is the accounting error of reading a change in how things are labelled as a change in where they are.

questions.explanation: Municipal finance turns on the cost of providing a service against the tax that district pays. Low-density expansion is expensive to serve because a road, a water main, a fire station and a refuse round all have to reach far fewer people than the same facilities do in a compact district, and a school may have to be built for a cohort that is still arriving. Meanwhile the tax yield per hectare is usually lower at the fringe, and a large share of a metropolitan area's property value is concentrated in the centre and in established inner suburbs. The result is a mismatch: the outer districts generate relatively little and consume relatively a lot, and unless there is a metropolitan authority to pool the money, the inner districts subsidise the fringe. The second option is the belief that networks are free to extend, and the fourth that costs and revenues scale together, which would only be true if the two had identical geometry. They do not, and the mismatch between them is the whole of the fiscal problem.

questions.explanation: A commuting shed is the labour catchment of a city: the set of places from which people travel in each day to work inside the urban area. It is a functional region, drawn by a daily movement rather than by a boundary, and it is held together by the transport that makes the daily journey possible. Where a railway, a high-frequency bus route or a motorway lane exists, the shed reaches much further out, because the generalised cost of a longer trip falls when the trip is fast and frequent. That is why the shed of a well-connected city is large and star-shaped, following the corridors, while a poorly connected one is a tight ring. The distinction matters for planning because the shed is where the region's housing demand actually sits, even where the region's people do not, and services have to be provided across it. The other options each attach the word to a different system, and none of them describes a daily labour market.

questions.explanation: Transit-oriented development works by putting enough people close enough to frequent transport that using it is the easy choice, and both halves of that sentence are load-bearing. Density supplies the passengers: a station every few minutes is only worth building and running if a lot of people live and work near it, and a low-density scatter of single houses around a station will not fill a platform. Accessibility supplies the rest: if the walk from home to the platform crosses a motorway, or the station is a car park with a roof on it, the density is not usable. A second requirement usually added in practice is a mix of uses, so that shopping and employment are close by as well as housing, and so the station is not purely a dormitory for commuters. The four options each keep one half and drop the other, which is the standard way this question is answered wrongly. The fourth is the most common practical failure, since parking is often built to attract a catchment and ends up consuming the land the density was supposed to occupy.

questions.explanation: The claim is about a change in behaviour, so the measurement has to be about whether people can and do reach a station without a car. Two conditions have to be checked together, because either can be satisfied alone and the claim can still fail. A development may put homes within a short distance of a platform while the only route is through a six-lane road, in which case nobody walks. It may also be genuinely walkable while the service is two trains an hour, in which case a car is still the sensible choice. The count that matters is therefore residents who satisfy both conditions, compared against the frequency of the service, since service is what sets the generalised cost of the trip. The other options each settle the matter with a figure that cannot detect the failure mode. A delivery count says nothing about accessibility, a footpath tally measures what was built rather than what is usable, and a jobs-and-homes net says nothing about how anyone travels.

questions.explanation: A disamenity is a land use that people would rather not live beside: noise, dust, odour, traffic, flood risk, or the prospect of change. The market mechanism is straightforward. Buyers price the disamenity into offers, so the price of the affected houses falls relative to comparable houses elsewhere, and lower-priced land is land that uses with a low bid for it can afford to occupy. Housing then sorts to where the air is clearer, which in a growing region is outward, and the industrial and nuisance uses concentrate in the remaining cheap land near the transport that makes them viable. Both halves of this matter. The price effect is what makes the sorting possible, and it also means that the households who end up beside a disamenity are disproportionately those who could not outbid others, which is why this pattern is a recurring theme in studies of environmental inequality. The second option has the mechanism backwards, and the fourth invents a cost condition the description does not supply.

questions.explanation: A buffer zone works by standing between a source of disamenity and the land that would otherwise be affected by it, so the thing that lowered prices there stops lowering them. The result is not that prices equalise but that the gradient shifts: land right against the railway still carries the disamenity, and land behind the trees does not, so the second is worth more despite being further from the station that may also be there. This is why a green strip beside a road or a railway is treated as infrastructure rather than decoration. The gradient it creates has a specific shape, rising steeply across the buffer and then flattening on the far side, and that shape is one of the ways a mapped buffer can be checked against the price data. The second option describes a barrier that transmits the disamenity, which is a screen designed to be seen through. The third confuses a shift with a cancellation, and the fourth mistakes a local effect on a boundary strip for a change in the region's total supply of land.

questions.explanation: The order runs from the market to the mechanism to the consequence and only then to the check, because each step depends on the one before it. Bid-rent theory starts with a competition: several users bid for the same plot, and whoever can make the most of it offers most, so the price at each point is set by the highest bid available there. Once that is established, the reason the bids differ by distance is the trade-off between land cost and travel cost, and beyond a certain radius the saving in land cost no longer covers the extra journey, so the bid falls. Once bids are falling, use follows bid, and housing, which needs the centre most, holds the expensive inner land while lower-value uses sort to the periphery. The last step is empirical rather than theoretical: the settled price at each band is the observable, and comparing it with the pattern is what confirms the account. Starting at the fourth step is the usual error, because a gradient drawn from prices alone can be described without ever being explained.
questions.hint: Begin with the competition that sets a price, then give the reason, the consequence, and the check.

questions.explanation: The dominant term is the surface energy balance. Urban materials such as asphalt, brick and concrete absorb short-wave radiation during the day, conduct it into the mass of the surface, and release it as long-wave radiation and as stored heat through the night. The countryside's vegetation and moist soils instead send a substantial part of the day's energy back as latent heat through evaporation, which cools the air locally. So the two surfaces differ both in how much heat they store and in how much they cool themselves, and the difference is largest on calm, clear nights when the stored heat is not mixed away. Industrial and vehicle waste heat is real and it is a measurable part of the budget, but it is a secondary term and it cannot explain a heat island over a park or a residential suburb, which is why the second option fails. The third is a real effect in particular basins, and the fourth would give a daytime radiation difference, not a night-time one.
questions.hint: Compare how the two surfaces use the energy they receive during the day.

That route is worth having because it uses the middle site, and a version of this question sometimes asks for the park-to-commercial difference alone, which is 4.5 and a different number. Comparing the commercial district with the park and reporting 4.5 measures a within-city gradient, not a heat island, because a heat island is defined against land that is not urbanised. The park reading is a genuine third quantity: urban green space usually sits between the rural reference and the built core, which is one of the reasons parks are worth having.

questions.explanation: Siting is a design decision that determines what a series measures, and it cannot be repaired by adding more of the same sites. A kerbside station sits in the space where traffic emissions are concentrated and dispersion is lowest, because the street canyon or the open road traps exhaust between buildings, so it is a measurement of roadside exposure. A resident fifty metres from that kerb, and almost every resident in a low-traffic residential street, experiences something lower, so the kerbside series reads systematically above the average experience. Adding more kerbside sites makes the estimate of roadside exposure more precise and leaves the bias exactly where it was. That is why a credible network pairs a rule-based series with a differently sited one, and the parkland comparison in the second option is doing real work rather than being an irregularity. The third option has the logic of the comparison backwards, and the fourth confuses the precision of an estimate with its representativeness, which is a distinction that holds in any sampling problem and not only in air quality.

questions.explanation: Placing a station next to the thing being measured maximises the signal, and that is exactly why the resulting number is not a population exposure. A monitor beside a busy road measures the concentration in the road's own air; a monitor on a roof in a residential quarter measures the concentration people there breathe. The two differ systematically, and the difference is a property of the design rather than of the weather on the day. The honest response is not to discard such a series but to state what it represents: near-source data are exactly what is needed to set an emission standard, to compare the effectiveness of two street designs, or to show which road to divert traffic from. questions.explanation: The protective function is a storage function. A wetland of open water, mud and low vegetation has a surface that sits below the level of a storm surge and a roughness that slows the water as it moves across, so a volume of water that would otherwise be conveyed to the sea in a few hours is impounded instead. Because the store fills and empties slowly, the water level behind it does not track the surge, so the peak that reaches the town is lower and arrives later. That delay is as valuable as the reduction, since it is often the difference between a road network that stays open and one that does not. The second option describes a sea wall, which resists rather than absorbs and which transfers the problem to somewhere else; the third and the fourth invent mechanisms that do not exist, since a wetland neither raises the ground nor cools the sea. The limit worth knowing is that the store has to be present and connected, and a wetland that has been severed from the sea by a road or a wall no longer performs this function.

questions.explanation: A food desert is defined by access, and access is a question about whether a household can get to a shop that sells a full range of food, expressed as travel time or travel distance. The word reasonably matters, and it is the part that has to be defined rather than assumed, because a distance is only inconvenient if the household has no way of covering it. A household without a car is differently placed from one with one, so most measures report the access level of the households least able to travel, and many compare it against a threshold set in minutes. The second option measures affordability, which is a different problem that can occur in the same neighbourhood, and the third counts outlets without asking whether anyone can reach them, so a neighbourhood with six shops none of which a resident can walk to would pass that test. The fourth is a budget share, and a household can spend a small share of its budget on food while still being unable to reach a shop. The policy response also differs between these, since a price problem is addressed with income support and an access problem with a location or a transport intervention.

The index therefore answers a question about distribution and refuses the question people most want answered, which is about place. answer.exemplar: A census tract is a small, relatively uniform statistical unit, usually built from a group of neighbouring blocks, that census agencies use so that very small areas can be described without disclosing the identity of the households in them. Its boundary is drawn with two aims in tension: on the one hand the tract should be internally similar in its social and housing characteristics, and on the other hand it should contain enough households, often a few thousand, that the published figures do not identify anyone. Any analysis that uses tract data has therefore inherited a geography that was designed for statistical confidentiality, not for the question being asked. The tract treats as homogeneous an area whose residents may experience the city quite differently, and it splits without regard for the functional geography of daily life, so a single workplace, a park boundary or a river can fall across several tracts and a single tract can contain two neighbourhoods. This is the modifiable areal unit problem in a concrete form. The same underlying pattern can look strong or weak depending on where the lines are drawn, so a comparison between two cities, or between two years, is only meaningful if the units have been made comparable, and a study that has not checked that should say so rather than reporting the difference as a fact about the cities.

questions.explanation: An explanation item of this kind has to make the definition and the consequence clear, because the definition is short and everything that matters follows from it. The crucial point is that a tract is a statistical unit, designed so that small-area figures can be published without identifying anyone, and it is not a unit of social or functional geography. Once that is stated, the two problems follow without further assertion: the boundaries cut across whatever units people actually live their lives in, and the same data can be grouped differently to produce a different picture. Students often answer this by describing the tract as a neighbourhood, which is the error the item is trying to surface, because a neighbourhood is a social and functional idea and a tract is a confidentiality device. A complete answer also notes the two competing design aims behind the boundary, since a tract that is too small cannot be published and one that is too large is not useful, and that the resulting tension is a permanent feature rather than a defect to be corrected in a later release.

questions.stem: A council states that its city is compact and polycentric, with all districts of similar density and no single dominant centre. A table of residents per square kilometre by district gives 9,400, 9,100, 9,250 and 9,350. What does the evidence show?
questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: A claim about a city's form

questions.explanation: The claim contains an internal contradiction, and the way to expose it is to name the area each part of the claim is measured over. Compactness is a statement about concentration, so it has to be assessed against the built-up area rather than against whatever administrative boundary happens to enclose the settlement. A figure of about 800 per square kilometre can only be produced by spreading a population over open country, and as soon as the claim's own numbers are read that way the city is spread over a wide footprint with density rising outward, which is the opposite of compact. So the low figure and the rising gradient cannot both be descriptions of the same built-up place. The first option is what makes this visible. The second, third and fourth each offer a comparison that would let the contradictory figure stand, and that is the trap: a relative or aggregate measure can usually be arranged to support a claim, which is why the denominator has to be pinned down before the numbers are read.
questions.hint: Ask what area each figure is averaged over before comparing them.
questions.learningObjective: identify which half of a form claim its own density data defeats

options.text: Low density must be stated against the built-up area, because a low average over a large boundary is not compactness
Low density must be stated against the national average, because only a relative figure describes a city
options.misconception: replaces the built-up area with an external comparison and misses the inconsistency

options.text: Low density must be stated against the rural reference, because only countryside values count as low
options.misconception: measures a city against farmland and so cannot contradict anything

options.text: Low density must be stated as a total, because only a population count describes a city's form
options.misconception: confuses population size with a measure of spatial concentration

questions.stem: A mayor claims a city is a compact, low-density settlement: density of about 800 people per square kilometre in the central district, rising to 2,600 in the inner suburbs and 5,100 on the outer edge. Which statement makes the claim assessable, and what settles it?
questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: The form claim the density data contradicts

questions.explanation: The sequence rises monotonically and steeply, from 1,100 at the centre to 6,200 at the edge, and a residential density gradient of that shape is not a real settlement pattern. In a city, the pressure to substitute space for proximity is greatest where land is scarcest and most accessible, so density falls outward, and the reverses of that pattern occur only where the units are not comparable or the boundaries are not where they are claimed to be. The usual cause is a table whose districts differ in area or in what they include, so the central figure is averaged over a large administrative area that contains parkland and countryside while the outer figure is averaged over a small, densely built one. That is a real possibility here and it is what the third option skips past: it treats a measurement artefact as a settlement structure and then invents a policy to explain it. The honest first step is to check whether the districts are drawn on the same basis and cover the built-up area, before reading anything into the gradient.
questions.hint: A rising sequence of this kind is a warning about the units before it is a finding about the city.
questions.learningObjective: read a reversed density gradient from a district table

options.text: Density rising with distance, which is not a real residential gradient and points to different units of area
Density falling with distance, which is the ordinary gradient and confirms the districts are comparable
options.misconception: reverses a monotonic rise into the usual fall

options.text: Density rising with distance, which shows a city whose centre has been deliberately depopulated
options.misconception: accepts the pattern as settlement and supplies a cause from nothing

options.text: Density constant in aggregate, so the four figures are really four measurements of one number
options.misconception: reports a rising sequence as a single invariant quantity

So the ring did what the previous item said it would: it held down nothing and moved the pressure outward. answer.exemplar: An urban place is a settlement where buildings are concentrated closely enough to form one settlement rather than scattered holdings, and the practical test applied is usually a density threshold on mapped parcels, so that urban land and rural land are adjacent rather than intermixed. The threshold is a matter of convention, which is exactly why the definition must be published and why the population figures that follow from it differ between authorities. One office may count only the continuous built-up area, and its urban population excludes everyone who lives in a village that is administratively part of the city. Another may count any settlement above a population threshold, which in a country of large villages brings in a great many people living in scattered form. A third may count whatever lies inside the administrative boundary of a city council, which includes farmland and woodland residents who are certainly not urban in any morphological sense. None of these is a calculation mistake. Each is a defensible answer to a different question, and the resulting national urbanisation rate can differ by many percentage points between them. The practical consequence is that a comparison of two countries' urbanisation rates is only meaningful once both have been computed on the same definition, and a comparison of one country over time is only meaningful if the definition has not been changed underneath the series, because a change in the method then appears as a change in the settlement pattern.

questions.explanation: This explanation is about a definition and its consequences, so the answer has to do both rather than only define. The definition itself is short and the analytical point is that the choice among reasonable definitions changes the measured quantity, which is why comparing figures compiled on different bases is meaningless. A strong response makes the three routes to a different figure explicit, because they are the concrete cases students meet when two sources disagree, and it explains that disagreement is a methodological artefact rather than an error to be corrected. It should also say what would make two figures comparable, which is that the same definition and the same threshold are applied to both, and what would quietly break a time series, which is a change in the definition part way through. The misconception to pre-empt is the belief that one of the authorities has it wrong and the other right: all three answers their own question correctly, and the mistake is to treat any of them as the answer rather than as one of several.
questions.hint: Give the definition, then show how each of two different rules changes the count.
questions.learningObjective: explain what an urban place is and why the definition has to be declared

answer.exemplar: The rank-size rule says that in a regular system of cities, the population of each city should be the population of the largest city divided by its rank, so the second city holds half as many people as the first, the third a third, the fourth a quarter, and so on. The regularity is not a law of nature but a statement of what is expected when cities are laid out as a system in which each centre serves the hinterland that requires it and no centre is arbitrarily favoured. The rule is used as a benchmark, and the interesting information is in the departures rather than in the fits. If the largest city is much larger than the second, and larger than the rule allows, the system shows primacy: a single city outweighing the rest of the system by a wide margin, which in most historical cases reflects the concentration of administrative, port or industrial functions at one point rather than an even national distribution of opportunity. If one of the lower ranks sits far below its prediction while the top ranks match, the departure points at that city, and a planner can ask what is different about its hinterland, its transport links, or its position relative to a larger neighbour. The indices used to measure this are all of the form observed size divided by predicted size, so a value above 1.00 marks a city larger than the rule expects and a value below 1.00 a city smaller.

questions.explanation: The answer has to cover the rule, the benchmark logic, and the direction of a departure, because each is a separate step and a response that stops after stating the rule misses the point of having a rule at all. The critical distinction is between a departure at the top of the system, which indicates primacy because primacy is by definition a property of the first city relative to the second, and a departure at a lower rank, which indicates something about that city's hinterland or its transport rather than about the shape of the whole system. Students often reverse this and read a small third city as evidence of a dominant capital, which cannot be right, since a dominant capital is exactly the case where the top ranks conform. The answer should also say why the rule is a conditional claim, so that a departure reads as information about a broken assumption rather than as a refutation, and it should be explicit that the index is a ratio against a prediction, because that is the form in which the figure is reported and the form in which it can be compared across ranks.
questions.hint: State the rule, then say which direction of departure means primacy and which does not.
questions.learningObjective: explain the rank-size rule and how a departure signals primacy

answer.exemplar: Density falls with distance from the centre because the value of being close rises as distance shrinks. Land near the centre is wanted for many purposes at once, and the people who can gain most from proximity are those who must make many journeys, so their willingness to pay for a central location is high, and the price of that land is set by the highest bid. Further out the same households can obtain more space for less money, and the saving in land cost eventually outweighs the cost of the extra travel, at which point their bids fall. Use follows bid, so housing holds the expensive inner land and progressively lower-value uses sort to the periphery. Sprawl changes the shape of this gradient rather than its direction. The decline is still monotonic, but the same low densities are found much further out, so the gradient becomes flatter and more extended, and the distance over which density falls to rural levels grows. This is why the gradient is measured rather than merely described, since the steepness of the fall is the quantitative signature of how compact a city is. The distinction matters for policy: a flatter gradient is the direct consequence of a population that grew more slowly than the area it occupied, and it is what low-density zoning and the provision of car infrastructure produce.

questions.explanation: This is a causal explanation, and the answer earns its keep by linking the mechanism to the measurable shape rather than describing the pattern and stopping. The chain to make explicit is proximity, then willingness to pay, then land price, then the use that can afford the land, so that the gradient is shown to follow from competition rather than from geography. Having established why density falls, the second half has to say precisely what sprawl alters: the slope becomes gentler and the fall extends further out, and the demographic signature is that footprint has grown faster than population. A common failure is to answer only the first half and treat the gradient as the whole of the topic, or to say that sprawl makes density fall faster, which reverses the measurable change. The explanation should also note that the gradient never inverts, because the uses that most need proximity keep the inner land however far the suburbs extend, so a table showing density rising with distance is telling you about the boundaries used to build the table rather than about the city.
questions.hint: Give the mechanism that produces the fall, then say what sprawl does to the slope.
questions.learningObjective: explain why density falls with distance and what sprawl does to the gradient

answer.exemplar: A dissimilarity index measures how unevenly two groups are distributed across the units of a region, by converting the count of each group in each unit into a share of that group's own regional total, taking the absolute difference between the two groups' shares in each unit, and halving the total. The index runs from 0, meaning that each group holds the same share of every unit, to 1, meaning that the groups are entirely separated. A value of 0.5 means half the population of one group would have to move for the two distributions to be made identical. What the index cannot show is anything about place, and there are two distinct reasons. The first is that it is blind to the arrangement of the units. Two regions can score identically whether each group is concentrated in opposite halves of the region with both groups mixed within districts, or whether they are concentrated in different districts of a single metropolitan area; the index is computed from shares alone and contains no information about where the units sit relative to one another. The second is that it is blind to how the pattern is distributed across units. An index of 0.5 can arise from every unit being mildly mixed or from a few units being completely segregated and the rest completely integrated, and these describe very different residential situations. It is also silent about change, since a single index carries no time dimension, and a pattern that is stable and one that is rapidly worsening can produce the same figure.

questions.explanation: The answer needs the arithmetic of the index, since that is what shows exactly which information has been thrown away, and then both reasons a given figure is ambiguous. The two reasons are distinct and both must appear: the index is invariant to how the units are arranged, and it is insensitive to how the segregation is spread across the units. A response that gives only the first will be marked down, because the second is the more misleading in practice, since a picture of a few wholly segregated districts and a picture of general but mild mixing look identical in the index and demand opposite policy responses. The closing point about the absence of a time dimension is worth making as well, because it explains why a single year's figure cannot be reported as a trend. The misconception to head off is the belief that a high index tells a planner where to act, which is precisely the inference the index refuses to support no matter how carefully it is computed.
questions.hint: Show what goes into the arithmetic, then give both reasons two equal figures can mean different things.
questions.learningObjective: explain what a segregation index measures and what it cannot show

answer.exemplar: A disamenity is a use whose presence lowers the value of the land around it, because it imposes a cost on the households there: noise, dust, odour, heavy traffic, flood risk, or the expectation that the site will change use again in a few years. The price effect is direct. Buyers bidding for a house beside the disamenity deduct that cost from what they will pay, and a developer building on the site prices the same deduction into the offer, so the affected land trades at a discount to comparable land that is free of it. The sorting that follows runs in two directions. On the land-use side, the discounted land is land that uses which can earn little per hectare can afford, so industry, warehousing, depots and scrapyards cluster in the cheap belt, and housing, which bids the most, is pushed to the clear land. On the household side, the households displaced from the clear land bid for the cheap land only when they cannot outbid anyone else, so the composition of the affected neighbourhood changes without anybody there having chosen to live beside the disamenity. The important consequence is that the association is a record of constraint rather than of preference, and it is why a neighbourhood beside a major facility is often inhabited disproportionately by households with low incomes, and why analysts of environmental inequality look at the joint distribution of hazards and income rather than at either alone.

questions.explanation: The answer has to run the mechanism in both directions, because sorting operates on land uses and on households, and a response that stops at the price effect has described a mechanism without a consequence. The steps to make explicit are the imposition of a cost, the discounting of bids, the resulting gradient, and then the two distinct movements that follow: uses that can earn little per hectare take the cheap land, and households that cannot outbid others are left in it. The distinction to hold on to is that neither movement is a choice made in the light of the disamenity, which is the point the item exists to make. A response that describes the sorting as residents preferring cheap land near industry has the direction of causation backwards, and one that reports only that prices are lower has not yet said who ends up there. The link to environmental inequality belongs in the answer, because it is the reason the pattern is worth measuring rather than only describing.
questions.hint: Follow the price effect through to both land uses and households, and be clear that neither chose the pattern.
questions.learningObjective: explain how a disamenity sorts land uses and households

questions.explanation: The order has to run from the pricing mechanism to the pressure on the fringe, then to the sorting that resolves the pressure, and only then to the check. Land prices are set first by the competition among bidders, and the households that place the highest value on proximity are the ones who can afford to bid most for the central land, so the price there is high by the time anything else has happened. As the city grows, that high-priced area is built out, and the land just beyond it becomes the new frontier: households who could not afford the centre find themselves travelling further, and the built-up area extends outward to meet them. Only once the pressure is placed does the sorting of uses appear, with the uses that can earn least per hectare taking the remaining cheap outer land and the housing corridor holding the land between the expensive centre and that outer belt. The final step is empirical, comparing the predicted pattern with measured prices and densities. Beginning with the check is the common error, and so is starting with the outer land, which presupposes a gradient it is supposed to be explaining.
questions.hint: Start with the bidding that sets a price, then the pressure on the fringe, then the sorting, then the check.

questions.explanation: The problem statement names two things to be changed and the intervention has to touch both. Concentrating permission where frequent transit already exists is what raises the share of households that can reach it without a car, and allowing homes, shops and work in the same district is what shortens the trips a household needs to make. Only then is the check meaningful, and it has to be the same two quantities that define the problem: the share of new housing within reach of frequent transit, and car journeys per resident rather than vehicles owned. Ownership is a poor proxy, because a household with two cars may travel less than a household with one that is a long way from anything. The other three options each substitute an output for an outcome, and two of them push demand further from the transit the problem identifies as scarce. The re-measurement matters as much as the instrument, since a policy that changed the location of housing but not the share of households able to reach a station has not done what the problem described.
questions.hint: Match the intervention to the two quantities in the problem, and re-measure those same two quantities.
